brief: Meaning-led Tincta Rewards concepts, retaining original Foldscape style and moderate complexity; intended associations are hypotheses to test.

prompts.name: Unfold
prompts.prompt:
Use case: stylized-concept / meaning-led identity artwork.
The attached original Foldscape is a STYLE reference, not a shape to preserve. Keep its precise angular folded planes, warm vermilion/orange/oxblood palette, optical depth through colored facets and sculptural energy.
This is identity artwork for Tincta Rewards: people collect permanent geometric NFTs; a sold-out collection has a verifiable draw; winning holders can claim a prize directly. Winning is conditional, not guaranteed. Do not put protocol diagrams, text or numbers into the artwork.
The user's priority is now MEANING: the shape should offer a recognizable first-glance association connected to rewards, with an original, refined folded-geometry treatment. The previous studies were too arbitrary and too minimal. Aim for a rich but readable composition with roughly 8–14 broad deliberate faces, enough internal rhythm to reward looking while retaining a strong avatar silhouette.
Square pure-white canvas, one artwork only, centered within a circular safe area about 76% of the square. No drawn circle, labels, names, letters, typography, wordmark, watermark, mockup, board or surrounding decoration.
Flat solid vermilion #FF3300, orange #FF6600, red #FF0000 and deep oxblood #330000. Crisp vector-like edges. Facet colors create implied depth; avoid gradients, glossy rendered materials, lighting, cast shadows, paper texture and photographic effects. No casino chips, money signs, upward profit arrows, Ethereum diamond, blockchain hexagon, cartoon treasure chest or generic crypto emblem.
Concept A — UNFOLDING REWARD.
Intended immediate association: opening, discovery, anticipation; something valuable is being revealed.
Draw a compact angular folded structure opening outward around ONE small vivid central polygonal facet. The outer planes should read as an unfolding enclosure, with three or four substantial articulated folds peeling back in unequal directions. The central reward facet is clearly separate, held in generous white negative space; use an irregular small pentagonal or trapezoidal form, not a diamond or a star. One broad lower fold acts as a shallow supporting cradle; two taller folds turn outward and back. The overall composition should suggest a prize being revealed without becoming a literal gift-box icon: no square box, no bow, no lid, no hands. It must visibly OPEN and REVEAL, rather than resemble unrelated floating shards. Use 8–12 intentional large facets and clean seams. Preserve the distinctive elegant tension of Foldscape, with an asymmetrical but composed outer silhouette, a visual focal point, and a legible open center. Moderate complexity, not extreme minimalism.

Concept B — FOLDED AWARD.
Intended immediate association: a prize, recognition, winning. The viewer should recognize the FAMILY of an award ribbon/rosette before noticing the inventive geometry.
Create an original folded-paper-inspired award emblem. Its upper mass is an irregular compact polygonal medallion made from a few broad interlocking folded bands, NOT a circular ring or repeated tiny petals. Give it a clear filled central face and 5–7 unequal angular rim folds. Two short asymmetric tapered ribbon ends emerge below from behind the medallion, each with a precise angular fold and a distinctive cut end. Make the overall proportions compact and substantial, rather than a long dangling medal. Use 10–14 broad colored faces total, with crisp vermilion/orange fronts and restrained oxblood returns. The folded geometry should look authored and dynamic, without a star, crown, wreath, trophy cup, numeral, laurel, coin border or military insignia. Avoid generic clip-art medal styling, uniform radial symmetry and decorative pleats. This is the conceptual next step of the supplied Foldscape: its facets now deliberately cohere into a recognizable award silhouette, refined enough for a serious contemporary brand.
